stage.title: So what next?
stage.prompt: If you ran PSLL in your own city next month, what would you keep, what would you change, and who would you invite to collect the data?

cards.title: Where a pop-up study like PSLL sits
cards.subtitle: Two restoration theories, one public-life tradition, and a realistic expectation of effect size.

blocks.p: Attention Restoration Theory (Kaplan, 1995) and Stress Reduction Theory (Ulrich et al., 1991) predict that settings with nature, shade, and seating should restore attention and lower physiological stress. Systematic reviews support the idea but find the attention benefits uneven across tasks: some measures improve consistently and others do not (Ohly et al., 2016; Stevenson et al., 2018).

At the population level, a meta-analysis of 143 studies links greenspace exposure with lower heart rate, diastolic blood pressure, and salivary cortisol, with associations rather than proven causal effects (Twohig-Bennett & Jones, 2018).
The observation side of PSLL comes from the public-life tradition: counting who stays, sits, and talks in a space (Whyte, 1980; Gehl, 1971/2011).

So what? A one-day, two-site intervention should expect small changes. The value is in triangulation: if behavior, self-report, physiology, and cognition point the same way, and each has different weaknesses, the conclusion is stronger than any single p-value (Lawlor et al., 2016).

cards.title: What to carry forward from this round
cards.subtitle: Measurement and reporting habits the literature says make a small study count.

list: HRV: record seated, at the same time of day, without talking, and report recording length and artifact handling (Task Force, 1996; Laborde et al., 2017). Recordings shorter than 5 minutes are "ultra-short" and need cautious interpretation (Shaffer & Ginsberg, 2017).
Heat changes HRV on its own (Bruce-Low et al., 2006). Keep the Frigga logger running at every site so PRE/POST temperature differences can be ruled out.

Report effect sizes with confidence intervals rather than significant/non-significant verdicts (Lakens, 2013; Cumming, 2014; Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016). Correct for the many metrics tested (Holm, 1979).
Check that observers agree with an ICC before pooling their counts (Koo & Li, 2016).

Nonrandomized before/after designs should follow the TREND reporting checklist (Des Jarlais et al., 2004) and name their threats to validity (Shadish et al., 2002). Participants who know the hypothesis may give the expected answer (Orne, 1962).
A shorter Perceived Restorativeness Scale still tells spaces apart (Negrín et al., 2017; Pasini et al., 2014), which matters when volunteers fill it in on a phone.

cards.title: Take it home: PSLL in your hometown
cards.subtitle: Every participant who repeats the protocol adds a site, which helps generalizability more than adding people to one site.

list: Pick a pair of spaces: one that gets a temporary intervention (seating, shade, planters) and one comparison space that does not. Run PRE and POST on the same weekday and at the same time of day.

Use the same instruments: observation sheets (4 × 5-minute snapshots), PANAS and the short PRS, a 3–5 minute seated Polar H10 recording, PVT and flanker tests via PsyToolkit, and a temperature/humidity logger.
Fill in the CSV templates in raw_data/templates and run the same pipeline. Identical column names let sites be pooled without hand-cleaning.
Record the public-life counts using the Public Life Data Protocol fields so they can be compared with city datasets (Gehl Institute, 2017).

blocks.p: With several hometowns, analyze site as a random effect: the question becomes "how much does the effect vary by place?" rather than "did it work in Space A?" Preregister the primary metrics before each new site so the pooled analysis stays confirmatory (Shadish et al., 2002). Each new site needs its own ethics approval or amendment.

cards.title: Going crowdsourced: a citizen-science PSLL
cards.subtitle: Phone prompts and wearables already let thousands of people report how places make them feel.

blocks.p: Experience-sampling apps show the format works at scale. Mappiness collected over a million momentary happiness reports from more than 20,000 people and found people happier in natural settings (MacKerron & Mourato, 2013). Urban Mind linked trees, sky, and birdsong to well-being in real time, with effects lasting hours after exposure (Bakolis et al., 2018).

Wearables add a physiological layer. Fitbit data from 8 million users showed HRV can be described at population scale (Natarajan et al., 2020). Smaller urban studies have paired wearables with GPS to relate crowding to stress responses while walking (Engelniederhammer et al., 2019).

list: Contributory: volunteers wear a sensor and answer phone prompts at any public space; the team analyzes.
Collaborative: volunteers also run observation sessions and help check data quality.
Co-created: residents choose which spaces to study and design the interventions themselves, the closest fit to a "living lab".

blocks.p: Open hardware such as the Smart Citizen Kit measures noise, particulates, temperature, and humidity and publishes readings openly (Camprodon et al., 2019). Low-cost sensors are good for relative and aggregated patterns but drift with weather and location, so they are not reliable as absolute measurements (Castell et al., 2017). Place one next to a reference logger like the Frigga at each site to calibrate it.

cards.title: Smartwatch or chest strap: what data is good enough?
cards.subtitle: Use the device that matches the claim: wrist HR for broad patterns, a chest strap for HRV.

list: The Polar H10 chest strap detected 99.6% of RR intervals correctly, matching or beating a clinical Holter ECG even during intense movement (Gilgen-Ammann et al., 2019). It remains the reference device for RMSSD.

Optical wrist sensors (Apple, Fitbit, Garmin and others) are reasonably accurate at rest, but error rose by about 30% during activity, and devices differed from each other (Bent et al., 2020). No significant skin-tone effect was found in that study, though earlier work had raised concerns.
In practice, crowdsourced smartwatch data can show heart rate during visits to a space. HRV claims should come from seated chest-strap windows, and device type should be recorded as a covariate.
Data access differs by device: phone health platforms export heart rate, but beat-to-beat RR data is often not exposed. Plan the export route before recruiting volunteers.

cards.title: Ground rules for citizen data
cards.subtitle: Heart data plus location is personal health data, even when collected by volunteers.

blocks.p: Citizen science raises four recurring ethical issues: data quality and integrity, data sharing and ownership, conflicts of interest, and the risk of exploiting volunteers' unpaid work (Resnik et al., 2015).

list: Consent should say exactly what is collected (HR/RR, GPS, survey answers), who sees it, and how long it is kept.
Publish aggregates only. Per-person heart data and precise locations can re-identify people. This dashboard's public copy stays on synthetic data for that reason.
Give results back to participants: their own PRE/POST change next to the group summary.
Each new site or recruitment channel needs ethics (IRB) review before data collection.
